title: Multivalued logarithm and principal logarithm
terms: complex logarithm; principal logarithm; logarithm branch; branch cut.

exposition.text:
Every logarithm of z ̸= 0 has form log |z| + i(Arg z + 2πk), k ∈ Z. The principal value is
Log z = log |z| + i Arg z. It is the imaginary part of this value, not its own argument, that lies in
(−π, π].
A holomorphic logarithm requires a consistent branch on a suitable domain. The usual princi-
pal analytic branch lives on C \ (−∞, 0] and has derivative 1/z. Principal logarithms need not
satisfy Log(zw) = Log z + Log w; the discrepancy can be an integer multiple of 2πi.
A branch is a single-valued choice that varies continuously (and, for an analytic branch, holo-
morphically) on its chosen domain. A branch cut removes a curve or ray so that such a consis-
tent choice becomes possible. The principal value assigns argument π to negative real numbers,
but jumps across that ray; the principal analytic branch therefore excludes the ray itself as well
as zero.

question.text:
3πi/4
Let z = w = e . What is Log z + Log w − Log(zw)?
(A) 0 (B) πi (C) −πi (D) 2πi (E) −2πi

solution.text:
The first two logarithms sum to 3πi/2. The product has principal argument −π/2, so its
principal logarithm is −πi/2. The difference is 2πi.

question.text:
2
For z ̸= 0, write θ = Arg z ∈ (−π, π]. For which θ does Log(z ) = 2 Log z hold?
(A) −π < θ ≤ π (B) −π/2 < θ ≤ π/2
(C) −π/2 ≤ θ < π/2 (D) 0 ≤ θ ≤ π
(E) θ = 0 only.

solution.text:
The real parts always agree. The imaginary parts agree exactly when 2θ already lies in
the principal interval (−π, π]. The asymmetric endpoint convention excludes −π/2 and
includes π/2.

question.text:
2+7πi/3
Using Arg ∈ (−π, π], what is Log(e )?
2
(A) 2 − 5πi/3 (B) e + πi/3 (C) 2 + 7πi/3 (D) 2 − πi/3 (E) 2 + πi/3

solution.text:
2
The exponential has modulus e and argument 7π/3 modulo 2π. Its principal argument is
π/3, so its principal logarithm is 2 + πi/3.

question.text:
L(z)
Can there be a continuous function L on the entire unit circle such that e = z at every point
of the circle?
it
(A) Yes, with L(e ) = it for every real t.
(B) Yes, and such L must be constant.
(C) Yes, if only real values of L are used.
(D) No, because the exponential has zeros.
(E) No, because a full circuit would change a continuous logarithm by 2πi at the same point.

solution.text:
it
If L existed, the continuous function [L(e ) − it]/(2πi) on [0, 2π] would be integer-valued,
2πi
hence constant. It would follow that L(e ) − L(1) = 2πi, although both arguments are
the same point. Choosing a principal value introduces a jump; it cannot give a continuous
logarithm on the whole circle.

question.text:
L(z)
On the slit plane C \ (−∞, 0], let L be analytic and satisfy e = z and L(1) = 4πi. What is
L(i)?
(A) 7πi/2 (B) 4πi (C) 5πi/2 (D) πi/2 (E) 9πi/2

solution.text:
Any analytic logarithm on this connected domain differs from the principal analytic
branch by a constant integer multiple of 2πi. The normalization gives L = Log +4πi, so
L(i) = πi/2 + 4πi = 9πi/2.
